Pre-underwriting

PU-01 / The red flag

When a bank denies good credit, the reason was on the credit report first.

If nobody reads that line before you apply, the bank finds the red flag before you do.

  • This sample report scores a 706. That's good credit, and the top line under the score is still a red flag.
  • The bank reads that line, and a good score doesn't change what it says.
  • When a bank says no to good credit, the reason was already sitting on the credit report.
  • Look at this sample report. TransUnion, FICO Score 9, a 706. That's good credit.
  • Now read the lines right under the score. The bureau prints the reasons that hold the score down, in its own words.
  • The top line says the balances on the cards are too high for the limits. That's the red flag.
  • The bank reads that line. A 706 doesn't change what the line says.
  • If nobody reads it before you apply, the bank finds it before you do, and you get the no.

PU-02 / The reasons

The top of your credit report lists the reasons a bank says yes or no.

  • The bureau prints them under every score, in its own words.
  • When a bank says no, the letter it sends gives those same reasons.
  • So the answer is sitting on your file before any application goes out.
  • Every credit report lists reasons under the score, and almost everybody scrolls right past them.
  • Those lines are what the bank weighs when it decides.
  • When a bank turns you down, the letter it mails gives those same reasons.
  • So the answer was on your file the whole time. It just has to get read before you apply, not after.
  • That's the first thing we do with every file. We read those lines first.
  • Your story: a client who showed you a denial letter, and the same reason was already on their report.

PU-03 / The cost

A no from a bank still costs you a hard inquiry.

  • Almost every application you send is a hard pull, and each one costs you.
  • The banks see the inquiries stack, and they start denying you.
  • This sample file already carries three, one on each bureau.
  • Here's what applying with that red flag costs you.
  • Almost every application you send is a hard pull, and each one costs you.
  • This sample file already carries three hard inquiries, one on each bureau: two card applications and a request for a higher limit.
  • A no from the bank doesn't take the inquiry back. It stays on your report, and the next bank sees it.
  • The banks see the inquiries stack, and they start denying you.
  • So an application with the red flag still on the file costs you twice: the no, and the inquiry that stays.
